title: Spark architecture -- Driver, Executors, lazy evaluation
exp: Every Spark performance question flows from understanding the Driver/Executor model and lazy evaluation. Understand this before writing a single line of code.
pts: Driver: coordinator. Runs your script, builds the execution plan, ships tasks to executors.
Executors: workers. JVM processes on cluster nodes. Read data, process tasks, write results.
Partitions: unit of parallelism. Each partition is processed by one task on one executor.
YARN (on EMR): resource manager. Allocates memory and CPU from the cluster pool.
Lazy evaluation: transformations (filter, select, groupBy) record what to do but do NOT execute until an action (show, collect, write) is called.
Catalyst optimizer: between your code and execution, Spark rewrites and optimizes the plan.
Shuffle: when Spark must redistribute data across partitions -- the most expensive operation.
code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = (SparkSession.builder
    .appName('OrdersPipeline')
    .config('spark.executor.memory', '4g')
    .getOrCreate())

df = spark.read.csv('s3://bucket/orders/', header=True, inferSchema=True)

# LAZY -- nothing executes yet
filtered = df.filter(df['amount'] > 1000)
grouped  = filtered.groupBy('category').agg({'amount': 'sum'})

# ACTION -- only now does Spark execute the full chain
grouped.show()

# See the physical plan BEFORE running
grouped.explain(extended=True)
# BroadcastHashJoin = no shuffle (fast)
# SortMergeJoin = shuffle (potentially slow)

viz.note: Driver (coordinator) sends tasks to 3 Executor boxes each processing partitions from S3. Shuffle arrows between executors at groupBy stage boundary.

qa.q: What is the difference between a transformation and an action?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Transformations (filter, select, groupBy, join) are lazy -- they build a DAG of operations. Actions (show, collect, count, write) trigger actual execution -- Spark optimizes the full DAG and submits tasks. Laziness enables optimization: Spark can push filters down and choose join strategies across the entire plan before executing anything.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Async methods compile into an IAsyncStateMachine struct managed by the AsyncMethodBuilder. Awaiting an uncompleted task yields execution back to the caller. Blocking with .Result on a thread bound to a SynchronizationContext causes deadlocks when the continuation waits for the blocked thread.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Sync-over-async (.Result or .Wait()) on ASP.NET request threads rapidly exhausts thread pool threads, leading to HTTP 503 gateway timeouts and request queuing under load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Async all the way preserves thread pool scalability, but requires passing CancellationToken through all layers and avoiding sync blocking methods everywhere.

qa.q: What is a shuffle and why is it expensive?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** A shuffle redistributes data across partitions so matching keys end up on the same executor. Occurs during groupBy, join, repartition. Requires intermediate files on disk and network transfer between nodes. The shuffle is the primary optimization target -- reduce its size (filter before groupBy), eliminate it (broadcast small tables).

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transient creates a new instance on every request; Scoped creates one instance per HTTP request container; Singleton lives for the app domain lifespan. Capturing a Scoped service inside a Singleton captures the DbContext across requests, causing concurrency bugs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Instantiating new HttpClient() instances manually causes socket exhaustion in OS TIME_WAIT state under high concurrency. Fix: register typed clients with IHttpClientFactory to manage handler lifetimes and DNS refresh.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** IHttpClientFactory prevents socket leaks and manages DNS rotation, but requires explicit Polly retry and circuit breaker policies to prevent cascade failures during downstream outages.
